subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: Guessing and grouping at the mela

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Can you make a guess?, p.64
tasks_in_class.description: Guess the number of triangular torans in the mela picture.
Count all the triangular torans by grouping in tens to verify the total.
Count the total number of bangles using Teji's counting strategy (groups of 10).
How many more triangles to make 300? How many bangles less than 300? Which is more: bangles or triangles?

time_bands.activity: Open the mela picture together. Children make a quiet written guess for Can you make a guess?, p.64 ("Guess the number of triangular torans in the mela picture...."). Share a few guesses aloud; notice the spread.

Children work in pairs on Now find out, p.64 ("Count all the triangular torans by grouping in tens...."). Each pair circles groups of ten on the page, then reports their count. Compare with earlier guesses.

Move to Try counting, p.65 ("Count the total number of bangles using Teji's counting strategy...."). Pairs apply the same grouping-in-tens strategy. A few pairs share their method; discuss why grouping helps.

Whole-class discussion on Let us Do, p.65 ("How many more triangles to make 300? How many bangles less than 300?...."). Children explain how they find the difference, linking the mela counts to approaching 300.

periods.teacher_notes: Encourage children to state their guess before counting — the contrast between a rough guess and a grouped count is the learning moment here. A common error is counting ungrouped objects and losing track; ask 'How did you make sure you didn't count one twice?' Watch for children who circle groups of ten but miscount the remaining loose objects.
materials: Pencils or crayons for circling groups

section_titles: Sequences and number patterns on tiles
periods.activity_title: Filling tile paths and arrow sequences beyond 200

tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the empty tiles on Jojo's tiled path with the correct numbers (sequences around 211–216, etc.).
Fill in blanks with correct numbers in three arrow sequences: (a) 294–310, (b) 227–234, (c) 382–390.
Guess how many ants there are; count and check. Discuss why different children get different answers.

time_bands.activity: Children work individually on Let us Do Q1, p.66 ("Fill in the empty tiles on Jojo's tiled path...."). After filling, pairs compare answers and correct any gaps.
Children tackle Let us Do Q2, p.66 ("Fill in blanks with correct numbers in three arrow sequences...."). Work through sequence (a) together as a class, then pairs complete (b) and (c) independently.

Children make a written guess for Let us Do Q3, p.66 ("Guess how many ants there are; count and check...."), then count the ants by grouping in tens. Pairs share their counts; class discusses why answers differ and how grouping-in-tens helps.

periods.teacher_notes: For the arrow sequences, children who learned to count large collections in groups of ten find the transition into the 300s straightforward — emphasise that the counting rule does not change when we cross a hundred boundary. A frequent error is writing 299, 300, 301 correctly but then writing 309 instead of 310; use the sequence aloud to let the rhythm catch the slip.

periods.activity_title: Matchstick bundles, expanded notation, and the number line

tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks: for each matchstick picture write the number and number sentence; for '300 and 16 more' and '109' draw matchsticks and complete the row.
Place the numbers from Q4 on the number line (0–350).

time_bands.activity: Hold up a bundle of ten matchsticks and a single matchstick; ask children to say the numbers shown. Briefly model how 2 bundles of 100, 3 bundles of 10, and 5 singles give 235, writing 200+30+5 on the board.
Children work on Let us Do Q4, p.67 ("Fill in the blanks: for each matchstick picture write the number and number sentence...."). Circulate; prompt children to count the bundle types before writing.
Children complete Let us Do Q5, p.67 ("Place the numbers from Q4 on the number line (0–350)."). Pairs discuss where to place 109 and 316, then the class shares placements on the board number line.

periods.teacher_notes: The key insight here is that a picture of bundles and singles translates directly into an expanded sentence — children who build this link confidently move between concrete and symbolic forms. A common error is writing 235 as 200+3+5 (counting tens bundles as single tens rather than groups of ten); ask 'Each ten-bundle holds how many?'
materials: A few actual matchstick bundles or rulers as substitutes

section_titles: Number slider: increase and decrease by 1, 10, 20
periods.activity_title: Making the slider and watching digits change

tasks_in_class.description: Look at six matchstick pictures and write the corresponding 3-digit numbers.
Make the number slider; use it to increase/decrease: (a) 285+1, (b) 147+10, (c) 367−2, (d) 289−10, (e) 290+20.

time_bands.activity: Children complete Let us Do Q6, p.68 ("Look at six matchstick pictures and write the corresponding 3-digit numbers."). Share answers; address any mismatch between bundle count and written digits before moving on.
Children construct the number slider from the textbook template. Support as needed; once built, each child dials in 285 and confirms it shows correctly.

Children work through Let us Do Q7, p.68 ("Make the number slider; use it to increase/decrease....") operations (a)–(e) at their own pace, recording the result each time. Pairs compare results and discuss which digit changed and which stayed the same.

periods.teacher_notes: The slider's physical action of scrolling one digit strip at a time makes it visible that changing a number by 1 affects only the ones strip, while adding 10 scrolls only the tens strip. Watch for children who scroll the wrong strip for +10 (a common error); ask them to point to the tens strip before they move it.
materials: Slider template from textbook (cut and assembled in class)

section_titles: Flag game: guessing a hidden number
Magical Count and extending hundreds on a number line
periods.activity_title: Flag guessing, magical letter chains, and 400 on the line

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Play — Flag game, p.69
tasks_in_class.description: Play the flag guessing game with a friend: one thinks of a number between 200 and 210, the other guesses using flag direction clues on the number line.
Write any number name, count its letters, write the name of that new number, keep repeating — what happens? Try with 187 and 204 as well.
Tell what the next hundred number is after 300; write it on the number line (0–400) and show it using matchsticks.

time_bands.activity: Pairs play Let us Play — Flag game, p.69 ("Play the flag guessing game with a friend: one thinks of a number between 200 and 210...."). One partner writes a secret number; the other guesses; the flag arrow gives a direction clue. Partners swap roles once.

Children work individually on Magical Count, p.70 ("Write any number name, count its letters, write the name of that new number...."). After finding the chain ends at FOUR with their own chosen number, they try again with 187 and 204. A few children share their chain on the board.

Whole-class: Numbers on a line, p.70 ("Tell what the next hundred number is after 300; write it on the number line (0–400)...."). Children write 400 on the printed line and sketch a matchstick bundle picture for 400 in their books.

periods.teacher_notes: In the flag game, children sometimes confuse 'flag points right' (number is too small, guess higher) with 'flag points left'; model one round on the board with explicit arrow directions before pairs begin. For Magical Count, let children choose their own starting word — the surprise that all chains land on FOUR is the reasoning reward; do not reveal it in advance.
materials: Scrap paper for Magical Count chains

section_titles: Locating numbers on number lines and distance reasoning
periods.activity_title: Placing numbers on lines and solving the sweet shop problems

tasks_in_class.description: Locate 216, 243, 257 on the number line (200–260).
Tell how far 387 is from 400 using the number line.
Which is more: 393 or 400? Use a number line and show by jumping how far 393 is from 400.
How many pieces of mysore pak are in one tray?
How many pieces of mysore pak are there in total?
Chacha is going to fill the tray with more laddoos. How many more laddoos will make the tray full?

homework.description: Locate 329, 332, 337, 375 and 387 on the number line (320–390).

time_bands.activity: Children work on Let us Do Q1, p.71 ("Locate 216, 243, 257 on the number line (200–260)."). Pairs share placement decisions; emphasise estimating position between marked hundreds.

Whole-class discussion of Let us Do Q3, p.71 ("Tell how far 387 is from 400....") and Let us Do Q4, p.71 ("Which is more: 393 or 400?...."). Children draw jumps on the number line to show the distance, then compare which number sits closer to 400.

Children read the Farooq Chacha sweet shop picture and answer Let us Do Q5(a), p.72 ("How many pieces of mysore pak are in one tray?"), Q5(b) ("How many pieces of mysore pak are there in total?"), and Q5(e) ("How many more laddoos will make the tray full?"). Circulate to check children count trays as groups of 100.

periods.teacher_notes: Children building on their experience of grouping in tens find that groups of 100 follow the same logic — emphasise that each full tray holds exactly 100. A common error in the distance questions is subtracting the wrong way round (computing 387−400 as a negative); encourage children to count forward from 387 to 400 using jumps on the number line. Additional sweet shop questions Let us Do Q5(c), Q5(d), Q5(f), Q5(g), p.72 make good consolidation homework or fast-finisher work.

section_titles: Hop Hundreds Home: apartment grid and place value
periods.activity_title: Reading the apartment grid and locating house numbers

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q1 (Hop Hundreds Home), p.73
tasks_in_class.description: Find the house numbers of the shaded houses without counting; fill in shaded boxes with correct house numbers.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q2 (Jump Joy Residency), p.74
tasks_in_class.description: Colour the houses to which Arvind Dada has to deliver sweets: 209, 228, 242, 258, 267, 276, 290, 315, 346, 367, 389, 395.
Write the floor and column number for each of: 13, 67, 106, 159, 192, 231, 245, 328, 380, 399.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the apartment grid: count aloud the columns (ones) and floors (tens and hundreds) for one or two sample numbers so children grasp the layout before working independently.

Children complete Let us Do Q1, p.73 ("Find the house numbers of the shaded houses without counting...."). A few share how they figured out a shaded cell's number; reinforce column = ones digit, floor level = tens and hundreds.
Children work on Let us Do Q2, p.74 ("Colour the houses to which Arvind Dada has to deliver sweets...."). Pairs check each other's coloured cells.

Children complete Let us Do Q3, p.75 ("Write the floor and column number for each of: 13, 67, 106...."). Class shares answers for 106 and 231 to confirm understanding of how hundreds affect floor numbering.

periods.teacher_notes: The apartment grid makes the H-T-O structure of numbers spatially explicit — children who articulate 'the column tells me the ones digit' are ready for the more abstract tasks later in the section. A common error is confusing which direction increases tens versus ones; point to a neighbouring cell above and to the right and ask what changes.
materials: Coloured pencils or crayons for Q2

section_titles: Hop Hundreds Home: apartment grid and place value
periods.activity_title: Partial grid reasoning and 'Who am I?' digit riddles

tasks_in_class.description: Find and write house numbers in the blank spaces of the partial grid (given 12, 144, 238, 319); discuss how numbers change moving up/down and left/right.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q5 (Who am I? — card 1), p.75
tasks_in_class.description: Who am I? I have digits 9, 1 and 5. I am less than 200. I have 9 ones.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q5 (Who am I? — card 2), p.75
tasks_in_class.description: Who am I? I am a 3-digit number. I have only digits 4 and 0.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q5 (Who am I? — card 3), p.75
tasks_in_class.description: Who am I? I am greater than 300 but less than 400. I have no tens. My ones and hundreds digits are the same.

time_bands.activity: Children work on Let us Do Q4, p.75 ("Find and write house numbers in the blank spaces of the partial grid...."). After filling, pairs discuss: 'What happens to the number when you move one step right? One floor up?' Whole class shares the rule in their own words.

Children tackle Let us Do Q5, p.75, cards 1, 2, and 3 ("Who am I?...."). Encourage children to write down their reasoning for each clue before committing to an answer. Discuss card 3 together — the 'no tens' constraint — since children often struggle to write a zero in the tens place.

periods.teacher_notes: The partial grid task consolidates the column-and-floor rule developed in the previous section of the apartment grid work; children who articulate the pattern in words ('go right, add 1; go up, add 10') are ready to extend it. A frequent error in the 'Who am I?' riddles is ignoring the order of constraints — children write 159 for card 1 without checking 'less than 200'; ask them to apply each clue in sequence and cross-check.

section_titles: Dienes blocks: drawing H-T-O for 3-digit numbers
periods.activity_title: Drawing Dienes blocks, patterns in grids, and Clap-Snap-Pat

tasks_in_class.description: Draw Dienes block representations for house numbers 309, 275, 423, 365, 343, 458, 562, 606, 800; write types of boxes/packets and number sentence.
How many boxes of 10 fit in: (a) 1 box of 100, (b) 2 boxes of 100, (c) 4 boxes of 100, (d) one opened box of 100?
Play Clap-Snap-Pat: record hundreds (clap clap), tens (snap), ones (pat) in the table; given 211 is done, record four more numbers.

homework.book_ref: Let us Do Q9 (Number hunt), p.78
homework.description: Write all numbers between 200 and 300 that have 5 as a digit (Is 245 one such number? Write the others).

time_bands.activity: Children complete Let us Do Q6, p.76 ("Draw Dienes block representations for house numbers 309, 275, 423...."). Emphasise drawing the zero-tens case (309, 606) and the pure hundred (800) — children who skip the tens column make a place-value error.

Whole class works through Let us Do Q8, p.77 ("How many boxes of 10 fit in: (a) 1 box of 100...."). Children write answers and then say in their own words the relationship between a box of 100 and boxes of 10.

Class plays Let us Play — Clap-Snap-Pat, p.78 ("Play Clap-Snap-Pat: record hundreds, tens, ones...."). Teacher calls a number; children perform the body-movement sequence and then fill in the table. Four numbers beyond the given example are recorded.

periods.teacher_notes: Drawing Dienes blocks for numbers with a zero in one position (309, 606) is where children most often make a place-value error — they omit the tens column entirely rather than drawing a zero there; ask 'How many tens boxes did you draw? Write that digit in the tens place.' The Clap-Snap-Pat game reinforces the same H-T-O decomposition in a kinesthetic register, giving children who struggled with the drawing a second route to the same idea.
materials: Open space or room to stand for Clap-Snap-Pat

periods.activity_title: Spring Leap patterns and the Show and Tell chain

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q7(a) (Spring Leap Homes), p.77
tasks_in_class.description: Write the house numbers of the yellow and pink houses in the Spring Leap Homes grid.
Write the pattern you see in the yellow and pink house numbers.
Create a chain of cards: each card states a number and asks 'Who has …?'; distribute, read aloud, and identify the answer chain.

time_bands.activity: Children work on Let us Do Q7(a), p.77 ("Write the house numbers of the yellow and pink houses...."). Pairs list the numbers they find and order them.
Children complete Let us Do Q7(b), p.77 ("Write the pattern you see in the yellow and pink house numbers."). Small groups share the pattern they articulate; whole class agrees on a description.

Class makes Show and Tell cards, p.78 ("Create a chain of cards: each card states a number and asks 'Who has …?'...."). Each child or pair writes one card; cards are distributed and the class reads the chain aloud in sequence.

periods.teacher_notes: For the Spring Leap Homes pattern, children who have worked through the apartment grids in the Hop Hundreds Home section of the chapter often spot the diagonal pattern quickly — push them to describe it in words ('each step diagonally increases by…'). For Show and Tell, pre-agree a set of numbers children will use for their cards so the chain forms a complete loop; a gap in the chain is a useful diagnostic for which number gave trouble.
materials: Small blank cards or cut paper for Show and Tell

tasks_in_class.description: Compare using > or <: (a) 199 and 201, (b) 285 and 275.
Think and match: link each comparison statement (a)–(f) to the correct reason (six pairs).
Make all 3-digit numbers using digits 3, 2, 4 without repeating; colour the greatest red and smallest yellow.
Arrange from smallest to biggest: 456, 389, 207, 99, 110.

time_bands.activity: Children complete Let us Do Q1, p.79 ("Compare using > or <: (a) 199 and 201, (b) 285 and 275."). Pairs share their reasoning: which digit did they look at first and why?

Children work on Let us Do Q2, p.80 ("Think and match: link each comparison statement (a)–(f) to the correct reason."). Class discusses one matched pair together, then children finish the remaining pairs independently.

Children complete Let us Do Q5, p.81 ("Make all 3-digit numbers using digits 3, 2, 4 without repeating; colour the greatest red and smallest yellow."). Pairs check they have listed all six arrangements.

Children tackle Let us Do Q7(a), p.81 ("Arrange from smallest to biggest: 456, 389, 207, 99, 110."). Share the strategy — notice that 99 and 110 are not 3-digit numbers — and discuss what happens when numbers have different digit counts.

periods.teacher_notes: The worked examples in the comparing numbers section of the chapter show the hundreds-first strategy clearly; children who apply it to Q1 consistently should carry it into Q2's matching. A common error is placing the > symbol the wrong way ('open mouth faces the smaller number' is a useful reminder). For Q7(a), note that 99 is a 2-digit number — fewer digits always means smaller — and surface this before children attempt to compare digit by digit.
materials: Red and yellow crayons for Q5

items.section_title: Counting beyond 200
items.prompt: There are 247 beads in a box. Show how you would count them by making groups of ten. Draw circles to show the groups and write the total.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 24 groups of ten (240 beads) and 7 loose beads; total is 247.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Group objects in tens, count the groups as hundreds and tens, then add the remaining ones.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may use actual counters to form physical groups; those who finish quickly count a collection of 263 objects the same way.

exercise.description: Count all the triangular torans by grouping in tens to verify the total.

items.section_title: Dienes blocks: drawing H-T-O for 3-digit numbers
items.prompt: Draw the Dienes block picture for the number 304. Then write the number sentence that matches your drawing.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 large blocks (hundreds), 0 flat strips (tens), 4 small cubes (ones); number sentence: 300 + 0 + 4 = 304.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify how many hundreds, tens, and ones are in the number and draw the matching block for each.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Let struggling learners use the matchstick bundle pictures from the chapter to decide how many of each block to draw; ask fast finishers to draw the blocks for 406 and write its number sentence.

exercise.description: Draw Dienes block representations for house numbers 309, 275, 423, 365, 343, 458, 562, 606, 800; write types of boxes/packets and number sentence.

items.section_title: Counting beyond 200
items.prompt: There are 286 buttons in a jar. How many more buttons are needed to make 300? How do you know?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 14 more buttons are needed, because 286 + 14 = 300.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count on from 286 to 300, keeping track of each step.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may use a number line to count the jumps from 286 to 300; ask those who finish to also say how many buttons would be needed if the jar had 293.

exercise.description: How many more triangles to make 300? How many bangles less than 300? Which is more: bangles or triangles?

items.section_title: Sequences and number patterns on tiles
items.prompt: Three children each count a pile of seeds. Priya gets 218, Renu gets 221, and Dev gets 215. They all counted the same pile. Why might they get different answers?

options.label: A
options.text: Only one child can count seeds correctly — the others must be wrong.

options.label: B
options.text: The number of seeds is too big to count so any answer is fine.

options.label: C
options.text: The seeds changed their number while the children were counting.

options.label: D
options.text: They each used groups of ten but some seeds may have been counted twice or missed.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option A — even when grouping in tens, seeds can be accidentally skipped or counted twice, giving slightly different totals.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recognise that counting errors arise from losing track; grouping carefully in tens reduces but does not always eliminate the error.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The child does not understand that a collection is fixed; they think the objects themselves can change.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child holds a misconception that counting has one authoritative performer, not that the method matters.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child has given up on counting as a reliable tool for large numbers — address this by showing that grouping makes counting manageable.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Let struggling learners physically recount a small set of 30 objects in pairs and compare totals; ask fast finishers to explain what strategy would give the most reliable count.

exercise.description: Guess how many ants there are; count and check. Discuss why different children get different answers.

items.section_title: Matchstick bundles and number sentences
items.prompt: A matchstick picture shows 2 bundles of 100, 0 bundles of 10, and 6 single matchsticks. Write the number this picture shows. Then write the number sentence (expanded form) for it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The number is 206. Number sentence: 200 + 0 + 6 = 206.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the hundreds bundles, tens bundles, and singles; write their values and add them.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may look at the matchstick bundle table in the chapter to remind themselves of the bundle values; ask fast finishers to draw the matchstick picture for 'three hundred and eight'.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks: for each matchstick picture write the number and number sentence; for '300 and 16 more' and '109' draw matchsticks and complete the row.

items.section_title: Number slider: increase and decrease by 1, 10, 20
items.prompt: A number slider shows 263. You move the tens strip down by one step (decrease by 10). Which digit changes?

options.label: B
options.text: Only the ones digit changes — it becomes 262.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the tens digit changes — it becomes 253.

options.label: D
options.text: The hundreds digit changes — it becomes 163.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option A — decreasing by 10 scrolls only the tens strip, changing 263 to 253.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: On the number slider, each strip controls one place value; moving the tens strip changes only the tens digit.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child confuses decreasing by 10 with decreasing by 1; they are scrolling the ones strip instead of the tens strip.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child has confused which strip controls which place value, assigning the tens change to the hundreds position.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The child believes any change to a number must affect all its digits — they have not yet understood independent place values.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Let struggling learners use the physical slider to perform the move before answering; ask fast finishers what number would result from decreasing 263 by 20.

exercise.description: Look at six matchstick pictures and write the corresponding 3-digit numbers.

items.section_title: Flag game: guessing a hidden number
items.prompt: Tara thinks of a number between 300 and 310. Mohan guesses 305 and the flag points right (too small). He then guesses 308 and the flag points left (too big). What numbers could Tara's number be? Write all the possibilities.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The number must be greater than 305 and less than 308, so it is either 306 or 307.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the two clues to narrow the range: the number is greater than 305 and less than 308.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may mark 305 and 308 on a drawn number line and identify the numbers between them; ask fast finishers to make their own flag game with a secret number between 410 and 420.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Play — Flag game, p.69
exercise.description: Play the flag guessing game with a friend: one thinks of a number between 200 and 210, the other guesses using flag direction clues on the number line.

items.section_title: Magical Count and extending hundreds on a number line
items.prompt: Start the Magical Count with the number 'sixty'. Count the letters in the word 'sixty', write the name of that new number, and keep going. What number name does the chain always reach? Write each step of your chain.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: sixty → 5 → five → 4 → four → 4 → four (the chain reaches FOUR and stays). Steps: sixty (6 letters) → six (3 letters) → three (5 letters) → five (4 letters) → four (4 letters).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the letters in each number name, write the new number name, and repeat until the chain settles.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may count letters on their fingers for each word; ask fast finishers to start the chain from 'two hundred' and show it also reaches FOUR.

exercise.description: Write any number name, count its letters, write the name of that new number, keep repeating — what happens? Try with 187 and 204 as well.

items.section_title: Locating numbers on number lines and distance reasoning
items.prompt: Look at the number line below. How far is 362 from 400? Count the jumps and write your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 362 is 38 steps away from 400 (400 − 362 = 38).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count forward from 362 to 400 on the number line, or subtract 362 from 400.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may draw small jumps of 1 from 362 to 400; ask fast finishers how far 362 is from 350.

exercise.description: Tell how far 387 is from 400 using the number line.

items.section_title: Hop Hundreds Home: apartment grid and place value
items.prompt: In an apartment building, house number 135 is on floor 13, column 5. What is the house number one floor above 135? What is the house number one step to the right of 135? Explain how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One floor above 135 is 145 (add 10); one step to the right of 135 is 136 (add 1).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Moving one floor up adds 10 to the house number; moving one column right adds 1.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may draw a small section of the grid around 135 to see the neighbours; ask fast finishers what house number is two floors above and three steps to the right of 135.

exercise.description: Find and write house numbers in the blank spaces of the partial grid (given 12, 144, 238, 319); discuss how numbers change moving up/down and left/right.

items.section_title: Hop Hundreds Home: apartment grid and place value
items.prompt: I am a 3-digit number. I am greater than 300 but less than 400. I have no tens. My ones and hundreds digits are the same. What number am I?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 303. The hundreds digit is 3 (since the number is between 300 and 400), the tens digit is 0, and the ones digit equals the hundreds digit, so it is also 3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply each constraint in order: hundreds = 3, tens = 0, ones = hundreds digit = 3, giving 303.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Let struggling learners write the H-T-O boxes and fill in what they know from each clue one at a time; ask fast finishers to make up their own 'Who am I?' riddle for a classmate.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Q5 (Who am I? — card 3), p.75
exercise.description: Who am I? I am greater than 300 but less than 400. I have no tens. My ones and hundreds digits are the same.

items.section_title: Number hunt, patterns, and 100-10 relationships
items.prompt: Arvind Dada opens 3 boxes of 100 sweets each. He wants to repack all the sweets into small boxes of 10. How many small boxes of 10 will he fill exactly?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 30 small boxes, because each box of 100 fills exactly 10 boxes of 10, and 3 × 10 = 30.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the relationship 1 box of 100 = 10 boxes of 10; multiply by 3 to get 30.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child thinks 1 box of 100 = 1 box of 10, ignoring the size difference entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child confuses the total count of sweets (300) with the number of boxes needed, not applying the grouping-by-10 step.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child adds 10 and 3 rather than multiplying, suggesting they do not yet see the repeated-grouping structure.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may draw 3 large squares (boxes of 100), each split into 10 strips (boxes of 10), and count all the strips; ask fast finishers how many boxes of 10 would come from 5 boxes of 100.

exercise.description: How many boxes of 10 fit in: (a) 1 box of 100, (b) 2 boxes of 100, (c) 4 boxes of 100, (d) one opened box of 100?

items.section_title: Number hunt, patterns, and 100-10 relationships
items.prompt: Look at the house numbers in a diagonal of the Spring Leap Homes grid: 11, 22, 33, 44. Write the next two numbers in this diagonal pattern. Describe the pattern in one sentence.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The next two numbers are 55 and 66. The pattern increases by 11 each time (add 10 for one floor up and add 1 for one step right).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each diagonal step adds 10 (floor up) and 1 (column right) simultaneously, so add 11 each time.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may draw the grid cells and fill in each number step by step; ask fast finishers to describe the diagonal pattern starting from 15.

exercise.description: Write the pattern you see in the yellow and pink house numbers.

items.section_title: Comparing numbers using > and <
items.prompt: Which symbol correctly fills the blank? 317 ___ 371

options.label: D
options.text: Both > and < work depending on which number you start from.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option C — 317 < 371 because both numbers have the same hundreds digit (3), but 1 ten is less than 7 tens.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare hundreds first (equal), then compare tens: 1 ten < 7 tens, so 317 < 371.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child sees the same digits in both numbers and concludes the numbers are equal, without attending to the order of the digits.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child has reversed the comparison or confused the direction of the < symbol.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child misunderstands comparison as relative to a starting point, not as an absolute relationship.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may use Dienes block pictures to 'see' which number is larger before writing the symbol; ask fast finishers to write three more pairs of numbers using the same digits in different orders and compare them.

exercise.description: Think and match: link each comparison statement (a)–(f) to the correct reason (six pairs).

items.section_title: Comparing numbers using > and <
items.prompt: Using the digits 5, 1, and 8 (each used once), make all possible 3-digit numbers. Write them in order from smallest to greatest and circle the greatest.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The six numbers are 158, 185, 518, 581, 815, 851. In order from smallest to greatest: 158, 185, 518, 581, 815, 851. The greatest is 851.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare hundreds digits first; within the same hundreds, compare tens digits to order correctly.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may write each combination on a separate slip of paper and physically sort them; ask fast finishers to also circle the smallest and explain why it is smallest.

exercise.description: Make all 3-digit numbers using digits 3, 2, 4 without repeating; colour the greatest red and smallest yellow.

items.section_title: Sequences and number patterns on tiles
items.prompt: Which number correctly fills the blank in this sequence? 296, 297, 298, ___, 300

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option B — 299, because the sequence counts on by 1 each time.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify that each term is 1 more than the previous; the number after 298 is 299.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has gone backwards instead of forwards, subtracting instead of adding.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child skipped 299 and jumped directly to 301, not noticing the blank falls before 300.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child added 10 instead of 1, confusing the step size in the sequence.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may count on from 296 using their fingers; ask fast finishers to continue the sequence up to 305.

exercise.description: Fill in blanks with correct numbers in three arrow sequences: (a) 294–310, (b) 227–234, (c) 382–390.

items.section_title: Matchstick bundles and number sentences
items.prompt: Which number is shown by: 1 bundle of 100, 4 bundles of 10, and 7 singles?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option A — 147, because 1 hundred + 4 tens + 7 ones = 147.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write the value of each bundle type in its place: H=1, T=4, O=7 gives 147.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child swapped the tens and ones digits, writing 174 instead of 147.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child placed the ones value in the hundreds position, scrambling the place values.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child reversed all three digits, reading the number right-to-left.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may draw the bundles and singles and label each group before writing the number; ask fast finishers to write the expanded number sentence for 147.

exercise.description: Place the numbers from Q4 on the number line (0–350).

items.section_title: Locating numbers on number lines and distance reasoning
items.prompt: Mark the number 234 on the number line below with an arrow and label it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 234 should be marked roughly 34 units along the line from the 200 mark, clearly between 200 and 250 and closer to 250 than to 200.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Locate 234 by starting at 200 and counting 34 steps toward 250.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may count small jumps of 10 from 200 (to 210, 220, 230) and then count 4 more; ask fast finishers to also mark 218 on the same line.

exercise.description: Locate 216, 243, 257 on the number line (200–260).

items.section_title: Hop Hundreds Home: apartment grid and place value
items.prompt: In the apartment building, the ground floor starts at house number 01. Each column to the right adds 1 and each floor up adds 10. What house numbers are in column 7 on floors 0, 1, 2, and 3? Write all four numbers.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Floor 0: 07; Floor 1: 17; Floor 2: 27; Floor 3: 37.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Column 7 gives ones digit 7; each floor up adds 10, so floor 0→07, floor 1→17, floor 2→27, floor 3→37.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may draw a small strip of the grid for column 7 and fill it in step by step; ask fast finishers what house numbers appear in column 7 on floors 4 through 7.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Q2 (Jump Joy Residency), p.74
exercise.description: Colour the houses to which Arvind Dada has to deliver sweets: 209, 228, 242, 258, 267, 276, 290, 315, 346, 367, 389, 395.

items.section_title: Comparing numbers using > and <
items.prompt: Arrange these numbers from smallest to biggest: 312, 89, 203, 412, 132.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare hundreds digits first; 89 has no hundreds, so it is smallest; then order the 3-digit numbers by hundreds, then tens.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may sort cards with each number written on them physically before writing the sequence; ask fast finishers to also arrange the same numbers from biggest to smallest.

exercise.description: Arrange from smallest to biggest: 456, 389, 207, 99, 110.

items.section_title: Locating numbers on number lines and distance reasoning
items.prompt: A tray holds 100 pieces of barfi when full. There are 67 pieces on the tray now. How many more pieces are needed to fill the tray?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 33 more pieces are needed (100 − 67 = 33).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the current count from the full tray capacity: 100 − 67 = 33.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may count forward from 67 to 100 on a number line; ask fast finishers to find how many more pieces are needed if the tray currently has 84 pieces.

exercise.description: How many pieces of mysore pak are in one tray?

items.section_title: Locating numbers on number lines and distance reasoning
items.prompt: Chacha has a tray that holds 100 laddoos when full. Right now, 63 laddoos are in the tray. He adds more laddoos to fill the tray completely. How many laddoos does he add? How many laddoos are in the tray now?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: He adds 37 laddoos (100 − 63 = 37). The tray now has 100 laddoos.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the current count from 100 to find how many more are needed; the full tray holds 100.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling learners may count jumps from 63 to 100 on a number line to find the difference; ask fast finishers to solve the same problem if the tray holds 100 and currently has 48 laddoos.

exercise.description: Chacha is going to fill the tray with more laddoos. How many more laddoos will make the tray full?
